title: Frustrated? Angry? Why these Nova Scotians say you should scream it out
summary: A group of Nova Scotians now meet weekly to scream their frustrations into the ocean. From grocery prices to global instability, they say there's plenty to motivate them these days.

image.caption: Kristen Parker started the Bedford Scream Club as a way to meet people and let out her frustrations about the world. They meet once a week in a park to scream together. (Carolyn Ray/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
A group of Nova Scotians now meet weekly to scream their frustrations into the ocean. From grocery prices to global instability, they say there's plenty to motivate them these days.
Atlantic Voice examines the growing trend of screaming as therapy in documentary
On a cold September night in Bedford, N.S., six people line up on the boardwalk and gaze out at the basin. Then, they scream for one minute straight.
“This is a form of meditation,” said Kristen Parker, who founded the Bedford Scream Club. “It just looks very different.”
A few months ago, these people were strangers. But now, they’re friends united by their passion for letting out their frustrations with a group scream.
Parker decided to start the weekly meet-ups in the summer. She’s originally from Louisiana, and as a woman in her 40s, she struggled to meet people when she moved to Nova Scotia.
A friend back home told her about similar scream clubs in cities across the United States, and she felt inspired.

“One of the things that I think is cool about screaming is the fact that you can show up and it’s very, very low pressure. You’re not expected to have a conversation with a stranger, you’re just expected to show up,” Parker said.

The club meets every Sunday night and screams precisely at 7 p.m. with the blessing of the police station nearby. The timing is strict, so officers know that’s the one scream they don’t have to respond to.
The frustrations underpinning the group scream are wide-ranging. Members list a number of things that rankle them including politics, global instability, climate change and grocery prices.
“I really hate that there are people who don’t have access to health care, things like that,” said Parker. “That leads me to scream.”
Tyler Morrison, lead singer of the metal band Last Call Chernobyl, finds screaming to be cathartic. He says he feels empowered when he performs. (Carolyn Ray/CBC)

The idea of screaming on a regular basis is something Tyler Morrison wholeheartedly supports. The self-described “bit of an introvert” transforms in his evenings as the lead singer of the Halifax-based metal band Last Call Chernobyl.
He said while most people think that screaming as a side passion is depressing or sad, for him it’s the opposite.
“I feel like I could move the Earth,” he said. “It’s just raw power.”
The band just returned from its first international tour, performing across China for a few weeks in the fall.
The experience was eye-opening, said Josh Pellerin, Last Call Chernobyl’s drummer.
He said they didn’t know what to expect, especially given the language barrier. But he said screaming is what united the band and the fans.
He sees it as a universal language to create a connection.

“Having them screaming along with us was just nothing short of life-changing,” Pellerin said. “Halfway across the world, you have people who love the technique, love the music. There’s no other way to explain it.”
Josh Pellerin, drummer for Last Call Chernobyl, says screaming gave the band a way to connect with their fans in China. (Carolyn Ray/CBC)
It may feel good for the band to scream, but there’s little research on scream therapy.
American psychologist Arthur Janov wrote a book released in 1970 called The Primal Scream. He suggested screaming as a way to let out repressed feelings from childhood.

It became briefly popular — John Lennon was among its proponents — but the theory has been debated by other experts, with some warning it can backfire by causing the body to seize up after letting out a burst of endorphins.
That’s why Elise Besler suggests alternatives to her clients.
Besler is a somatic voice coach based in Halifax, N.S. She’s not a registered therapist, but teaches people how to connect their voices to their bodies with a trauma-informed approach.
“I believe that our voices are medicine,” Besler said. “Just the way they vibrate through ourselves and our nervous system, the science tells us that our nervous system is soothed.”
She understands why people might connect with screaming, as it mimics that first moment when a baby is born, and people wait for a baby to let out a cry.

“That’s our first nature, and I believe so many of us are just trying to get back to that first nature because of lived experience and culture and all the things that really keep us from being fully expressed,” she said.

Elise Besler helps people feel empowered through their voices. Instead of screaming, she suggests people do full body grunts to release frustration. That way they won't damage their vocal cords. (Carolyn Ray/CBC)
While screaming might work for some, she worries that people may damage their vocal cords if they don’t do it safely.
Besler prefers letting out full body grunts with people punching their hands away from their bodies to release frustration. She also uses straws to blow bubbles in water while humming.
“Expression isn’t just from our throats, it’s from our entire bodies.”

For the Bedford Scream Club, it all boils down to adding some whimsy into their lives at a time when the world is full of stressors. And so, they continue to meet each Sunday for a little release, inviting anyone nearby to join in.
Robert Darling, a member of the club, suggests people just give it a go.
“You can be any age to scream. Heck, I’m 73,” he said.
“It isn’t governed by age, it’s governed by who wants to have fun. If you can scream away and have fun, why not?”
